# Shape as a Precondition {#sec-shape-precondition}

Part I has been about objects: what the distribution of a price change looks like, what a
coastline's roughness does when you change the ruler, what memory does to a random walk. This
chapter converts all of it into something Part II can use, and the conversion is the argument of
the chapter.

The conversion is this. **A claim about shape should enter a decision as a precondition, not as a
conclusion.**

The difference is not semantic. It is bookkeeping, and the reason bookkeeping matters is that a conclusion is something a reader is entitled to rely on while a precondition is something the reader is obliged to check against their own circumstances before it can be used. A conclusion is a thing you have established and can build on. A
precondition is a thing you are assuming, which has a scope, a duration, and a failure mode that
must be specified before it can be used. Most of the damage in applied risk work comes from
treating the first as the second.

## Three ways a shape claim gets used

The same sentence — "returns are fat-tailed" — does three different jobs depending on where it
sits.

**As a finding.** It reports a property of a dataset, with a method and a scope. Harmless here. This is where the
sentence belongs in a paper, and where it does the least damage.

**As a modelling assumption.** It licenses a particular family, a particular estimator, and a particular set of tools, which is a large commitment to make on the strength of a sentence. This is where it earns its keep, and where its scope must travel with it.

**As a decision constraint.** Here it changes behaviour, which is why the bookkeeping that accompanies an assumption in its second role has to travel with it into its third role, or the decision inherits a licence that was never granted. It changes what you are willing to do: how much you will hold, what
kind of insurance you will buy, which instruments you will avoid. This is where it is most useful
and where it is most often misapplied, because the sentence arrives without its scope.

The mistake is not using a shape claim in the third role. It is using it in the third role without
the second role's bookkeeping.

## The shape sheet

The book's proposal here is a small piece of paperwork. For any shape claim you intend to act on,
write four lines.

**Claim.** The sentence, in the form it was established. "Daily returns of large-capitalisation
equity indices have tails thicker than Gaussian over the period 1926–2020."

**Scope.** Where it was measured, and over what range of scales. If the claim came from a paper,
the range is in the paper. If you cannot find it, the claim has no scope and you do not have a
precondition.

**Duration.** The period over which you are willing to assume it still holds. This is a judgement,
and it is the line most often left blank. A claim about 1926–2020 is not a claim about next year,
and the difference is not small.

**Failure mode.** What you will do if the claim turns out to be false. A precondition without a
failure mode is a belief.

Four lines. The first two are easy. The last two change behaviour. Most practitioners can write the
first two from memory. Writing the third forces the admission that a historical regularity has a
shelf life, and writing the fourth forces a plan for being wrong.

## The sheet in use

An example with an irreversible component, worked through the four lines.

A firm is considering a long-term supply contract with a single counterparty. The engineering is
sound and the price is favourable. Losses if the counterparty fails are bounded by the prepayment,
but the firm becomes dependent on that counterparty for a critical input, and switching costs rise
with time.

**Claim.** The counterparty is financially stable and the input will remain available at
competitive prices.

**Scope.** Stability was assessed from the counterparty's audited accounts and three years of
delivery record; the market for the input has two other qualified suppliers at present.

**Duration.** Five years, which is the contract term. The judgement here is that the counterparty's
accounts are informative for about two years and the supplier market for longer, so the duration is
set to the shorter of the two horizons rather than to the contract.

**Failure mode.** If the counterparty defaults in year four, the firm has a prepayment exposure and
no qualified alternative. That is not survivable at the current scale. **The sheet, having reached
this line, has changed the decision:** the answer is not to avoid the contract but to bound the
exposure — shorter terms, staged commitments, or a second qualified supplier developed in parallel.

The point of the example is the fourth line. The first three could be written by any competent
analyst. The fourth is the one that detects an expose whose failure is not survivable, and it does
so without any probability estimate.

## Applying it to the three claims of Part I

Three worked examples, using the material of the preceding chapters.

**Claim one: prices have thicker tails than the Gaussian model allows.**

Scope: daily and monthly returns of liquid markets; tails characterised by an exponent that can be
estimated over the top few percent of observations. Duration: unchanged in character since the
1960s, though the estimated exponent moves with the method. Failure mode: if returns are Gaussian
after all, the cost of the mistake is over-insurance, which is paid in small increments.

**Claim two: roughness is scale-invariant over two to three decades in geographic and market
series.**

Scope: stated range only. Duration: structural, since the generating processes — erosion,
heterogeneous participants — change slowly. Failure mode: outside the range, the exponent is not
defined, so decisions that assume scaling beyond it are unsupported.

**Claim three: long memory is present in volatility and contested in returns.**

Scope: contested, and the estimates depend on the estimator. Duration: unknown. Failure mode: using
a long-memory model for pricing, which the previous chapters showed to be structurally invalid
because the process is not a semimartingale.

The third example is the interesting one. It is also the reason the sheet has four lines. The claim
is in a state where scope is unavailable and duration is unknown. Under the sheet's rules, it
cannot enter as a precondition. **It can be used as a hypothesis to be tested, which is a different
role with a different bookkeeping standard.**

## Objection: this is ordinary risk management

The sheet looks like a checklist for counterparty risk, and the objection is that the discipline
already exists under other names.

The difference is what happens when the estimate is unavailable.

Ordinary risk management requires a probability, or a distribution, or at least a score. When the
probability cannot be estimated — the case from the previous interlude — the practice degrades into
assigning a qualitative label to a number, which is how a judgement becomes a figure that looks
computed.

The sheet does not require a probability at any line. It requires a scope, a duration, and a
failure mode, all three of which are properties of the decision and the situation rather than
estimates of the world. **That is the point: the discipline is available precisely where estimation
is not.**

## The duration line, examined

Duration is the line left blank most often, so it is worth saying what can support it. Three things. Three things.

**Mechanism stability.** Physics-based regularities last longer than behavioural ones, because the
mechanisms change more slowly. A roughness exponent in a geological series has a longer expected
life than a return regularity in a market.

**Institutional stability.** A regularity that exists because of a rule lasts as long as the rule,
and rules change on political timescales. Many market regularities are of this kind, which
dramatically shortens their duration.

**Statistical evidence.** A stability test across subperiods is evidence, and it is weaker than it
looks when the subperiods are few or the statistic is noisy — as Part I showed for exponents.

Where none of the three is available, the correct duration line reads "unknown", and the claim
cannot enter as a precondition. That outcome is common, and writing it down is more useful than
inventing a number.

## What makes a shape claim usable

From the three examples, a short list. A shape claim can carry a decision when:

- its scope is stated in the form it was measured;
- the transformation it survives is named, in the sense of Chapter 1's grades;
- its duration is either argued or explicitly flagged as an assumption;
- the cost of being wrong is stated and is survivable.

None of these is exotic. All four are usually absent. All four are routinely absent, and the fourth is absent most often. **A
precondition whose failure is unsurvivable is not a precondition; it is a bet with the stakes
hidden.**

## What Part II takes from Part I

Part II turns from objects to standards, and it inherits four things.

**A taxonomy of failure.** Three ways a number fails, and the diagnosis determines the remedy.

**A reporting convention.** Exponents travel with their windows, and the rule has been applied to
every exponent in this book.

**A distinction between grades of robustness.** Claims survive specified transformations, or they
do not, and the grade should be stated.

**A habit.** Ask over what range, and ask what happens if the answer is wrong.

The next chapter opens Part II with a paper that begins from exactly this position: an author
dividing the world into cells according to the kind of uncertainty involved, and then arguing that
the standard tools apply in three of the four.

## Claim and tool

The claim: shape claims used as preconditions require scope, duration, and a failure mode, and
claims lacking these cannot carry decisions.

The tool: the four-line sheet, and the rule that a claim without a failure mode is treated as a
belief rather than a precondition.

Both are the book's. The sheet is deliberately modest. It is a form, not a theory. It is a form, and forms are what
organisations use when a practice needs to be checkable by someone other than the person doing it.

## Boundary conditions

The sheet applies to decisions that are repeated or that carry irreversibility. For a single,
reversible decision taken once, the paperwork exceeds the stakes.

It presumes that scope can be stated. Some shape claims arise from qualitative observation rather
than measurement, and for those the sheet's second line cannot be completed, which places the claim
outside the decision procedure rather than inside it.

And it does not tell you what duration to assume. That is a judgement about the stability of the
world, not a calculation, and pretending otherwise would be the same error the sheet exists to
prevent.

## Three ways a shape claim fails to be usable

The chapter's earlier material states what makes a shape claim usable. This section states the three
ways such a claim can fail to be usable even when it is true, because each has a different remedy and
confusing them wastes effort.

**The claim is true but unmeasurable at the relevant horizon.** Wrong horizon. Use the ordinary machinery. The tail is genuinely fat, and the
decision's horizon is short enough that the fatness has almost no effect on the relevant
probabilities. The remedy is not better measurement. It is to notice that the shape claim is
irrelevant to this decision and to use the ordinary machinery, with the awareness that the horizon
matters.

**The claim is true and measurable but the mechanism is unknown.** Common case. No extrapolation. The statistic is stable, the range
is documented, and nobody can say what generates it. The claim is usable for prediction in the
measured range and unusable for extrapolation, because extrapolation requires knowing that the
mechanism persists. **This is the most common state of an empirical regularity, and treating it as a
licence to extrapolate is the most common error of the three.**

**The claim is true, measurable, and mechanistically understood, but the mechanism is under pressure.** Watch the constraint. A regularity produced by a regulatory constraint lasts as long as the constraint. The
claim is usable, its duration is estimable from the durability of the constraint, and the monitoring
requirement is to watch the constraint rather than the statistic. This is the regime Chapter 25
treats in detail, and it is the only one of the three cases where a precise duration can be stated
with a reason.

**How to tell them apart.** One question. Ask it first. One question, applied to whatever the shape claim is being used for:
**what would have to stay the same for this to keep working?** If the answer is "the data-generating
process, at a horizon I have measured", the first case applies. If the answer is "something I can
name but not verify", the second. If the answer is "a rule or constraint with a known institutional
life", the third.

**Why this distinction matters here.** Because a precondition
without a stated duration is a claim about the future disguised as a description of the present, and
the disguise is what makes shape claims feel more solid than they are.

## From claim to precondition in four steps

This chapter has argued that a shape claim must be usable before it can be a precondition. That argument
has four steps, and they are worth stating as a procedure.

**Step one. State the shape claim with its range.** Not "the tail is fat" but "the tail index is below
three over the range measured, by these two methods".

**Step two. State the duration and its basis.** Mechanism stability, institutional stability, or
statistical evidence. **Where none is available, write "unknown", and the claim cannot enter as a
precondition.**

**Step three. State the failure mode of the decision.** What happens if the deviation is larger than
assumed. Where the answer is a bounded loss, the precondition is a preference. **Where the answer is an
absorbing state, the precondition is a requirement and the bounding moves come first.**

**Step four. State what would falsify the precondition.** An observable event — a rule change, a
publication, a capacity threshold — that would move the claim out of the usable category. **A
precondition without a falsifier is a belief with a number attached.**

**What the four steps produce.** A page. The claim, its range, its duration with a reason, the
consequence of being wrong, and the event that would overturn it. **That page is what the rest of the
decision can be built on, and building it takes an hour.**

**Why the social mechanism matters here.** The fourth step is where a project's sponsors discover that
the precondition has an expiry date, and the discovery is usually unwelcome. **Writing the date down
before the commitment is the whole of the technique.**

## When the precondition fails after the decision

A precondition is a claim with a duration, and the interesting case is the one where it fails while the
position is open. The response is the final part of the discipline and the one least planned.

**Three failure paths.**

**The mechanism changes.** Abrupt path. A rule is altered, a market structure shifts, a population's composition changes.
**This is the abrupt path and the one that the leading indicators of Chapter 25 are designed to pre-empt.**

**The estimate was wrong.** Gradual path. The range or the exponent was misjudged, and the deviation appears as the position
being more dangerous than assumed. **This is the gradual path and the more common one.**

**The range stops covering the horizon.** Invisible to statistics. The precondition was true over its stated range, and
the range is no longer the relevant one. **This path is invisible to statistics and detectable only by asking
whether the range still covers the decision's horizon.**

**What to have written down before the position opened. Three lines.**

**The indicator.** One observable. What observable would tell you the precondition has failed.

**The threshold.** Failure, not noise. How much deviation constitutes failure rather than noise.

**The action.** Written in advance. What the position becomes when the threshold is crossed.

**Why the third line is the one usually missing.** Because the action is a decision, and writing a decision
before the position exists feels like pre-empting a judgement. **It is the same objection the pre-committed
exit meets, and the answer is the same: the judgement made now, unemotionally, is better than the judgement
made later by someone with a position to defend.**

**What to do if none of the three was written.** Impose them now, in writing, with a date. **A precondition
without a monitoring specification is a claim that will be replaced silently, which is how positions are held
past the point where their justification has expired.**

## A precondition checklist for a proposal

The chapter's four steps are a procedure. Compressed, they are a checklist for anyone presenting a proposal whose
justification includes a shape claim.

**Four lines, on one page.**

**The claim, with its range and its method.** Not "returns are fat-tailed" but the quantity, the range, and the
two estimators.

**The duration, with its basis.** Mechanism stability, institutional stability, or statistical evidence. **Where
none is available, write "unknown", and the proposal has no precondition and must be argued on other grounds.**

**The failure mode of the decision.** What happens if the precondition fails while the position is open. **A
bounded loss is a preference; an absorbing state is a requirement.**

**The trigger.** The observable whose appearance would require re-examination.

**What the checklist changes about a proposal.** It converts an assumption into a monitorable condition. **A
proposal carrying the four lines can be approved with a review date; one without them can only be approved on
confidence in the proposer.**

**What a reviewer does with it. Three questions.**

Is the range the same range as the decision's horizon. **A precondition measured over the wrong range is a
precondition for a different decision.**

Is the mechanism cited one that exists, or one that would explain the pattern if it existed. **The distinction
between a mechanism and a hypothesis is frequently blurred in proposals.**

Is the trigger observable without new measurement infrastructure. **A trigger that requires a new data collection
is not a trigger.**

**Why the checklist is short.** Because the alternative to a short checklist is a longer section of the proposal
that the reader skips. **Four lines on the first page are read; four pages in an appendix are not, and the
placement is part of the discipline.**

## Three preconditions and their durations

A precondition is a shape claim plus a duration. Three kinds of duration appear in the book's material, and each
is estimated differently.

**Mechanism stability. The longest.** A regularity produced by a physical or structural mechanism lasts as long
as the mechanism. **Estimated from the mechanism's nature: a roughness exponent in a geological series has a
longer expected life than a return regularity in a market.**

**Institutional stability. The life of a rule.** A regularity produced by a fee schedule, a settlement convention
or a regulation lasts as long as the rule. **Estimated from the rule's political or contractual life, which is
often knowable from documents.**

**Statistical stability. The shortest and the least informative.** A regularity supported only by its history,
with no mechanism identified. **Estimated from the record's length, which is a lower bound on nothing in
particular.**

**What the three imply for a precondition's statement. One sentence each.**

**Mechanism.** "This holds as long as the mechanism does, which is expected to be decades." **Which is a claim
about physics and is checkable in principle.**

**Institution.** "This holds as long as the rule stands, and the rule is up for review in two years." **Which is
checkable from a document and gives a monitoring date for free.**

**Statistics only.** "This has held over the measured period and no mechanism has been identified." **Which is
the honest statement and the one that keeps the claim out of the precondition role.**

**Why the third case cannot serve as a precondition.** Because a precondition requires a reason to expect
continuation, and a record supplies none. **Which is the chapter's central distinction: a shape claim is usable as
a precondition when it is indexed to something that can be monitored, and a record cannot be monitored.**

**What to do when only statistical evidence is available.** Treat the claim as an input to the analysis rather
than as a precondition, and use a structural instrument for the exposure. **Which is the same substitution the
book makes everywhere else, and it is why the ledger precedes the analysis.**

## The precondition and three ways it can be stated

A precondition is a shape claim with a duration. Three statements of it appear in the material, and each carries
a different amount of information.

**A bare shape claim.** "Returns are fat-tailed." **Which is a sentence in a paper and carries no range, no
duration and no failure mode.**

**A claim with a range and a method.** "The tail index is below three over the range measured, by these two
methods." **Which is checkable and is what a paper's methods section supports.**

**A claim with a duration and a failure mode.** "The tail index is below three over the measured range, the
regularity is produced by a settlement convention whose review is in two years, and the decision fails if the
index exceeds three." **Which is what a decision needs and is the form the chapter's checklist produces.**

**What the three statements cost. Increasingly more.** The first is free; the second requires the analysis; the
third requires knowing the decision. **Which is why the third is written by analysts who are close to the
decision rather than by researchers.**

**What the third statement adds. Two things.** The duration, from a named source, and the failure mode. **Both of
which are inputs to the monitoring specification rather than to the analysis.**

**How to move from the second to the third. One question.** What would have to stay the same, and what would tell
you it had not. **Which is the whole of the addition and takes ten minutes.**

**Why the third is what a proposal needs.** Because a proposal is a commitment over time, and a claim without a
duration cannot be committed to. **Three statements, and the third is the shortest route from a research result
to a decision that can be monitored.**

**What to do when the duration is unknown.** Write "unknown" and treat the exposure structurally. **Which is the
substitution the book makes everywhere and is preferable to a duration invented for the occasion.**

One claim. One duration. One failure mode. Write all three. Then it is a precondition.

## The precondition and three ways it fails to be useful

A precondition can be true and useless. Three failures appear in the material, and each has a different remedy.

**True and irrelevant to the decision's horizon.** The tail is fat over decades and the decision operates within
months. **The remedy is not better measurement: it is to notice that the claim does not bear on the decision and
to use the ordinary machinery.**

**True, relevant, and with no identified mechanism.** The statistic is stable over the relevant range and nobody
can say what produces it. **The remedy is to use the claim for prediction inside the measured range and to refuse
extrapolation, because extrapolation requires knowing that the mechanism persists.**

**True, relevant, mechanistically understood, and under pressure.** A regularity produced by a rule whose
continuation is contested. **The remedy is a monitoring specification aimed at the rule rather than at the
statistic, and this is the only one of the three where a duration can be stated with a reason.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is a case in which the precondition is not the binding
question. **Which is why the chapter's checklist asks for the failure mode rather than for more evidence.**

**How to tell them apart. One question.** What would have to stay the same for this to keep working. **The
horizon case answers "nothing, because the decision does not reach there"; the mechanism-less case answers
"something I cannot name"; the pressure case answers "a rule with a known review date".**

**Why the distinction matters for a proposal.** Because a proposal resting on the first case is over-documented;
one resting on the second needs a refusal of extrapolation written into its assumptions; and one resting on the
third needs a monitoring specification. **Three failures, three remedies, and only the third can be
scheduled.**

**What to do when the case is unclear.** Treat it as the second and refuse extrapolation. **Which is the
conservative reading and is available without knowing the mechanism.**

## The precondition and three kinds of monitoring

A precondition needs a monitor. Three kinds appear, and the differences determine what an organisation has to be
able to observe.

**Watch the statistic. The direct form.** Re-estimate the shape claim on a schedule. **Which requires the
estimation capability to persist and is the slowest of the three, since a changing exponent is visible in the
estimate long after the mechanism has moved.**

**Watch the mechanism. The fast form.** Observe the rule, the network or the physical system that produces the
regularity. **Which is faster and requires knowing what the mechanism is, and it is the form the chapter
recommends where a mechanism has been identified.**

**Watch the exposure. The structural form.** Track the position's worst case rather than the claim's input. **Which
requires no estimate at all and is available where the claim's status is uncertain.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is a schedule rather than an activity. **Which is what makes
a precondition monitorable: a claim that nobody is scheduled to re-examine is not a precondition but an
assumption.**

**How to choose among them. One condition.** Whether a mechanism has been identified. **Where one has, watch the
mechanism; where none has, watch the exposure and refuse extrapolation.**

**Why watching the statistic is the weakest.** Because it detects the failure after the position has been exposed
to it for the duration of the estimation lag. **Which is the same argument the decay chapter makes about watching
returns instead of the mechanisms, and it is the reason both chapters recommend the same practice.**

**What to record. Two items.** The monitor and the schedule. **Which is a clause and which is what turns a
precondition into a commitment that an organisation can keep.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The four-line sheet is a proposal, registered as part of the book's constructed material. There is
no literature testing whether such a form improves decisions, and I have not run the experiment.

The three worked examples use the material established in Chapters 1 to 6, and the scopes and
durations assigned to them are my judgements rather than findings. A reader who disagrees with the
duration assigned to the first claim is disagreeing about the stability of markets, which is the
right thing to disagree about.
